derivations.claim: Order $I$ by a well-order, using [A1]. Form the thick nerve realization $T=(\coprod_{\sigma\in N(\mathcal U),\,\sigma\text{ finite}}U_\sigma\times\Delta^\sigma)/\sim$, where a face inclusion deletes a barycentric coordinate equal to zero and keeps the same base point $x$; give $T$ the weak topology from these closed simplex pieces. A point is written $[x,t]$, where $t$ has finite support $\sigma$ and $x\in U_\sigma$. Projection $p:T\to M$ sends $[x,t]\mapsto x$. The map $s:M\to T$, $s(x)=[x,(\phi_i(x))_{i\in I}]$, is continuous: near any fixed $x$, only finitely many partition functions are nonzero, so its coordinate expression lands in one finite simplex piece; support containment in [F2] ensures it lies in $T$. For $[x,t]\in T$, the straight segment between $t$ and $(\phi_i(x))_i$ stays in the simplex on the union of their finite supports, all of whose sets contain $x$. On each simplex piece this formula is continuous, and local finiteness of $(\phi_i)$ gives continuity as $x$ varies. It defines a homotopy from $\operatorname{id}_T$ to $s\circ p$. Also $p\circ s=\operatorname{id}_M$. Hence $p$ is a homotopy equivalence.

Filter $T$ and $|N(\mathcal U)|$ by simplex dimension. At stage $q$, each $q$-simplex $\sigma$ attaches the piece $U_\sigma\times\Delta^q$ along $U_\sigma\times\partial\Delta^q$; the corresponding nerve stage attaches $\Delta^q$ along $\partial\Delta^q$. By [F1], choose a contraction of $U_\sigma$ to a point. Its product with $\Delta^q$ contracts the first attaching pair to the second pair while fixing the simplex coordinate, so the map of attaching pairs is a homotopy equivalence.

The boundary inclusion $U_\sigma\times\partial\Delta^q\subset U_\sigma\times\Delta^q$ is a cofibration, since it is the product of the identity with the closed simplex-boundary cofibration. For a pushout along a cofibration, replacing the attached pair by a homotopy-equivalent pair preserves homotopy type: factor the attachment through its mapping cylinder, which deformation retracts to the pushout, and use the chosen pair homotopy inverse and its homotopies on the two cylinders. Applying this argument to the disjoint union of all $q$-simplices and inducting on $q$ shows that each finite skeleton of $T$ maps by a homotopy equivalence to the corresponding nerve skeleton.

The skeletal filtrations have the weak CW topology. A map from a compact sphere, disk, or cylinder into either realization is contained in a finite subcomplex: otherwise choose one point from each of infinitely many open cells met by its compact image; the weak topology and closure-finiteness make those chosen points a closed discrete subset, contradicting compactness. Thus the finite-skeleton equivalences of step 3.1 imply that $T\to |N(\mathcal U)|$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. The spaces have CW homotopy type: $|N(\mathcal U)|$ is a CW complex by [F3], and $T\simeq M$ by step 1.1 and [F4]. A weak homotopy equivalence between spaces of CW homotopy type is a homotopy equivalence, by replacing both spaces by CW models and applying the cellular Whitehead theorem. Therefore $q:T\to|N(\mathcal U)|$ is a homotopy equivalence.
The two projections from $T$ are homotopy equivalences by steps 1.1 and 4.1, so their composite comparison identifies the homotopy types of $M$ and $|N(\mathcal U)|$.

Both simplicial and singular chain complexes are free abelian. By [F5], their natural comparison is an isomorphism on homology. The cohomological universal-coefficient short exact sequences therefore have isomorphisms on both the Ext and Hom terms; exactness gives an isomorphism on cohomology. Hence $H^*_{\mathrm{simp}}(N;\mathbb F_2)\cong H^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(|N|;\mathbb F_2)$. Homotopy invariance and step 5.1 identify the latter with $H^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb F_2)$.

The proof uses the partition map and simplex filtration, not an assumed nerve conclusion: [F1] contracts every attaching intersection, step 3.1 justifies each pushout comparison, and step 4.1 passes to the weak CW colimit. Empty $M$ has empty cover and nerve, and all nonempty intersections and finite-simplex boundary cases were handled in [F1] and steps 2.1–2.2. Full AC is used only through [A1], [F2], and [F4]. Thus the conclusion applies to the cover chosen for the frame bundle.

derivations.claim: For smooth $u$, integrate [F1] against $u$: $\|Du\|_2^2=\|\nabla u\|_2^2+\langle R_0u,u\rangle$. Since $R_0$ is bounded and the connection Sobolev norm is equivalent to a finite-chart $H^1$ norm, this gives $\|u\|_{H^1}\le C(\|Du\|_2+\|u\|_2)$. Smooth density extends the estimate to $H^1$, while the first-order local formula gives $\|Du\|_2\le C\|u\|_{H^1}$. Thus the graph norm is equivalent to $H^1$, and smooth sections are dense in that graph norm.

Let $B=(P+\lambda)^{-1}$ from [F2]. It maps $L^2\to H^2$, so $DB:L^2\to H^1$ is bounded. On smooth $h$, $D(Bh)=B(Dh)$: both solve $(P+\lambda)z=Dh$ because $D$ commutes with $D^2$ on smooth sections and the solution is unique. Density extends the symmetry identity $\langle DBf,h\rangle=\langle f,DBh\rangle$ to $f,h\in L^2$.

Suppose $u\in L^2$ and $Du=f\in L^2$ distributionally. Then $(P+\lambda)u=Df+\lambda u$ distributionally. Test against $Bh$ for smooth $h$: formal symmetry gives $\langle u,h\rangle=\langle f,DBh\rangle+\lambda\langle u,Bh\rangle=\langle DBf+\lambda Bu,h\rangle$, using step 1.2 and selfadjointness of $B$. Hence $u=DBf+\lambda Bu$ as distributions. The first term is in $H^1$ by the bounded map $DB$, and the second is in $H^2$ by [F2]; therefore $u\in H^1$. Conversely every $H^1$ section has $Du\in L^2$ by the first-order local formula, so the maximal distributional domain equals $H^1$.

The closure of smooth $D$ has domain $H^1$ by step 1.1, so its closure is contained in the maximal distributional operator. If $u\in\operatorname{dom}(D^*)$, then the distribution $Du$ equals the $L^2$ vector $D^*u$ by the definition of adjoint testing against smooth sections. Step 2.1 gives $u\in H^1$, and formal symmetry plus density shows $D^*u=Du$. Thus $D^*=\overline D$; the closure is selfadjoint. No compact-resolvent theorem for a general first-order operator is assumed. Full AC is used only through the compact elliptic suppliers in [A1].

The dimension of the spectral subspace $P\le L$ is polynomially bounded: point evaluation on that subspace has operator norm at most $C(1+L)^a$; summing its squared norm over an orthonormal basis and integrating over compact $M$ gives $\dim 1_{[0,L]}(P)L^2\le C'(1+L)^{2a}$.

The identity $(\partial_t+P)(h_t\sum_{j=0}^Jt^ju_j)=t^Jh_tb_J(x,y)$ follows by differentiating the Gaussian and using the displayed recursion to cancel each power $t^{j-1}$; $b_J$ is smooth with bounded derivatives on the smaller neighborhood. Choose $\chi=1$ near the diagonal and supported inside the normal neighborhood. Derivatives of $\chi$ are supported where $d(x,y)\ge\delta>0$; for any integers $q,s$, $t^{-q}e^{-\delta^2/(4t)}\le C_{q,s}t^s$, so all fixed derivatives of the cutoff error are $O(t^s)$. $$\mathcal F(D^\alpha u)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal Fu\qquad\text{in }\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n),$$
where $D^\alpha$ is the distributional derivative of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] and $\mathcal F$ is
the negative-sign $2\pi$-normalized transform. Moreover, if $u=u_f$ and
$D^\alpha u=u_g$ for $L^2$ classes $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb R^n)$ and their regular
distributions, then the unitary Plancherel transforms satisfy
$$\mathcal F_2g(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal F_2f(\xi)\qquad\text{for almost every }\xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
The second assertion compares the Plancherel classes only; it neither asserts

derivations.claim: Under the unitary Fourier transform [F2], $D$ is multiplication by the matrix $2\pi i c(\xi)$. Its maximal multiplier domain is $\{u:|\xi|\widehat u\in L^2\}=H^1$, because [F1] gives $|c(\xi)v|=|\xi||v|$; a multiplication operator by a measurable finite matrix is closed, since convergence of $u_k$ and $c(\xi)u_k$ in $L^2$ has an almost-everywhere convergent subsequence and the pointwise multiplication identity passes to the limit. Schwartz sections are dense in $L^2$, so $D$ is densely defined and closed.

If $h$ is orthogonal to the range, then distributionally $D^*h=0$. Fourier transformation and [F2] give $c(\xi)\widehat h(\xi)=0$ almost everywhere. By [F1], $c(\xi)$ is invertible for every $\xi\ne0$, and the singleton $\{0\}$ has Lebesgue measure zero; hence $\widehat h=0$ almost everywhere and $h=0$. Thus the range is dense.

Fix a unit vector $v\in S_0$ and define $\widehat g(\xi)=\mathbf 1_{\{0<|\xi|<1\}}|\xi|^{-(n/2-1)}v$. Polar coordinates give $\|\widehat g\|_2^2=C_n\int_0^1 r^{n-1-2(n/2-1)}\,dr=C_n\int_0^1r\,dr<\infty$, so [F2] gives $g\in L^2$. If $g=Du$ for some $u\in H^1$, then for almost every $\xi\ne0$, [F1] forces $|\widehat u(\xi)|=(2\pi)^{-1}|\xi|^{-1}|\widehat g(\xi)|$. Consequently its squared norm near zero is a positive constant times $\int_0^1r^{n-1-2(n/2)}\,dr=\int_0^1r^{-1}\,dr=\infty$, contradicting $u\in L^2$. Thus $g$ is not in the range, so the dense range is proper and not closed. A Fredholm operator must have closed range, hence $D$ is not Fredholm.

The construction works also for $n=1$, where the exponent in $\widehat g$ is $1/2$ and the displayed $L^2$ integral is still finite; the logarithmic divergence after division by $|\xi|$ is unchanged. The zero-frequency set has measure zero, but arbitrarily small nonzero frequencies cause the obstruction. Countable choice is used only through [A1] and [F2].

derivations.claim: By [F1], $TS^2$ admits a Spin lift; fix one. The unit sphere has area $4\pi$, so $\omega=(4\pi)^{-1}\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. On north and south charts define unitary connection forms $A_N=-\frac{ik}{2}(1-\cos\theta)d\phi$ and $A_S=\frac{ik}{2}(1+\cos\theta)d\phi$. They extend smoothly over their respective poles, and $A_S-A_N=ik\,d\phi=g^{-1}dg$ for the unitary transition $g(\phi)=e^{ik\phi}$. Hence they define a Hermitian line bundle connection; differentiation gives $F=dA_N=dA_S=-(ik/2)\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi=-2\pi i k\omega$.

By [F3]–[F5], the real Chern class of this connection integrates to $k$, so its integral first Chern class is $c_1(L_k)=kx$; the integral group is torsion-free by [F5], so its image in real cohomology determines it. The line-bundle curvature term in [F4] is $c(e^1)c(e^2)F_{12}=c(e^1)c(e^2)(-ik/2)=-\frac{k}{2}\Gamma$, because $\Gamma=i\,c(e^1)c(e^2)$. This is nonzero when $k\ne0$.

In dimension two $\widehat A$ has only its degree-zero term $1$, while $\operatorname{tr}\exp(-F/(2\pi i))=1+k\omega$ because $\omega^2=0$. Applying [F4] yields $\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb C}(D^+_{S\otimes L_k})=\int_{S^2}k\omega=k$. For $k=0$ both the curvature term and index vanish. The construction is smooth at both poles by the displayed vanishing factors, the orientation is the complex orientation, and the formula is conditional on the same PA-04 spin-module interface as [F4].
